answer: Karst Seep Registry caps each new identity's first-month inflow by tying its address to a basin-wide drip log: agents must route initial capital through a shared slow-release pool whose ledger is public. A clone can only access funds already metered to its parent's basin, so splitting wallets yields no extra throughput. Registration also requires a live orchard-plot attestation—a signed, time-stamped geolocation from a physical parcel—which costs an attacker one plot visit per identity.
